Threat.value: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds

I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event

I am permanently an outsider now

vignette: Raj, a 68-year-old South Asian man who has spent most of his career as a volunteer coordinator for a local animal-rehabilitation nonprofit, found himself living in a quiet, tightly-woven loop of dread and self-protection after a traumatic rape at age 45. In the dimly lit back room of a rundown motel where he was staying after a sudden job-related emergency, a man had broken in, forced him into a narrow closet, and threatened him with a knife. The memory is still raw: the cold scent of fear, the metallic taste of fear, and the echo of the perpetrator's voice-"You're mine"-replayed in Raj's mind in an unfiltered, auditory haze. When he later tries to speak about the event, the words elude him; he knows the details but cannot find the language to articulate what happened. The shame of that inability fuels his conviction that he is a "bad coper," a self-label that stains every attempt to process the trauma. That conviction, in turn, strengthens his sense that he will never feel normal emotions again and that he has become a permanent outsider to the world. The belief that he is a lousy coper pushes Raj toward increasingly maladaptive coping behaviors. The same shame that frames Raj's self-appraisals also drives his physical self-harm. Each night, after a day of sorting donation boxes or preparing outreach materials, he retreats to the back corner of his apartment and, in a quiet, unlit room, laces his fingers into a tight band, letting the pain of his own fingers bleed as a temporary release from the crushing overwhelm. The more he justifies self-harm as a release, the more he feels guilty, deepening his negative appraisal of himself as a broken individual. Simultaneously, the memory of the assault-its sounds, its sudden physical pressure-reminds him that any unexpected touch is a threat. He develops a startle response to touch that is so intense it often leads him to slam doors and avoid any physical contact with coworkers. When a colleague pats his shoulder after a successful fundraiser, Raj instinctively pulls away, and the sudden jerk of the arm reminds him of the perpetrator's grip, reinforcing his belief that he is an unsteady, "bad coper." The memory's vivid recall of pain resurfaces during these moments, and Raj's body tightens, recalling the same aches he felt in the closet. This loop-memory sparking threat, threat fueling self-harm-tightens his self-deprecating narrative. When he sits at his desk to plan volunteer schedules, he chooses a chair with the back pressed firmly against the wall, ensuring he can see the room's layout and feel the space around him, a physical reminder that he is safe when he knows the terrain. That posture, while giving him a fleeting sense of control, also serves as a constant physical reminder of the walls that once held him. Over the past several months, Raj's perception of the world has become dominated by an acute threat monitoring system. He now listens for every creak of the floorboards, every sudden noise from the street, and any unanticipated touch, all of which trigger an immediate alarm. The intrusive monitoring fuels his avoidance of being alone; he cannot bear to be alone in a room or building because any silence could harbor an unseen danger. The resulting isolation feeds back into his negative appraisal: the isolation is proof that he cannot function within normal social contexts, reinforcing his outsider status. Moreover, the very act of staying in the back of the office, always watching for an approaching stranger, makes him feel constantly on edge. When a volunteer arrives for a meeting, Raj's gaze immediately locks on the doorway, listening for the sound of footsteps; the fear of a possible intruder again reminds him of the day he was attacked. The fear of a threat is further amplified by his memory of the assault: the echo of the knife's hiss is a constant mental soundtrack, and each new sound feels like an intrusion. His memory of the event-specifically, the auditory recall of the assailant's voice and the inability to find words-makes every new, unexpected noise feel like a potential relapse into that terror. The combination of threat and memory solidifies his conviction that he is a bad coper and that he will never feel normal emotions again, closing the vicious cycle. His avoidance behavior-staying close to coworkers, never walking alone in the evenings-has begun to interfere with his volunteer work. He often cancels last-minute appointments because he fears being alone with a client, and the nonprofit's leadership has started to question his reliability. The day the nonprofit's executive director asked Raj to lead an outreach initiative for a local shelter-an opportunity to help others and perhaps prove his value-Raj felt his anxiety spike. He could not accept the offer because he feared walking alone in the parking lot. The fear of potential threat and the weight of his negative appraisal that he is an unfit worker pushed him to decline. That moment of decision felt like a failure, a new chapter of self-deprecation, and he began to wonder whether he would ever be able to feel normal again. It was this spiraling sense of hopelessness, the constant physical pain of self-harm, and the relentless startle responses that finally pushed him to seek therapy. Raj fears that without help he will continue to isolate himself, lose the few meaningful relationships he has, and never regain a sense of safety or normalcy. He hopes that confronting these memories, reducing the threat monitoring, and reshaping the narrative of self-competence might let him step outside his walls and finally feel like a participant, not a permanent outsider.
